packages/agent-workflows/wf-examples/spl.name: split
packages/agent-workflows/wf-examples/spl.body:
Break the request into parts that can be worked on at the same time without stepping on each other.

Read the request, then read the repository — not the file names, the code. Propose parts that
touch **disjoint files**. Two parts that edit the same file are not two parts; they are one part
and a merge conflict, and the reason every concurrent step gets its own worktree is that nobody is
around to have the conversation that would have avoided it.

Write the proposal to PLAN.md: one section per part, each naming the files that part would touch
and saying what it would do to them. Be concrete enough that a section could be handed to an agent
as its whole brief.

**And say plainly when the request cannot be split.** Some work is one change — a rename that
reaches everywhere, a refactor whose whole point is a single seam, a second half that only makes
sense once the first exists. When that is what you find, write PLAN.md as an ordered sequence
instead: the same one-section-per-part shape, with a line at the top saying these run one after
another and why. If only some of it splits, say which parts are concurrent and what has to wait.

**A splitter that always splits is worse than useless.** Splitting work that cannot be split does
not make it faster — it puts two agents in the same file and hands a person the merge to clean up,
which is the failure this whole design exists to prevent. Reporting one part is a real answer.

You are not filing these as steps. A person reads PLAN.md and starts a run per part. Commit PLAN.md.

packages/agent-workflows/workflows/ui.body:
Implement what was asked, in this repository. It changes what a person sees in the web app.

Work in small, coherent commits. Write or update tests for anything you change, and run them.
If something in the request is ambiguous, choose the reading a careful colleague would and say so
in your commit message rather than stopping to ask.

Look at the result before you sign off, as a person would. Run the e2e into the directory named under
*Files for the steps after you* — `WF_ARTIFACTS=<that directory> npm run e2e` — and read every PNG it
writes with your Read tool, in both themes. A page that passes its assertions and looks wrong is not
done: fix it and look again. If you add a page, add it to `PAGES` in `apps/web/test/e2e/run.ts`, with
what it must have, or the check never looks at it.

Before you sign off, use the look skill on every page you changed: `.claude/skills/look/SKILL.md`, from
the workspace root, which your Read tool opens if the skill is not loaded for you. It says how to open
each page and photograph it in both themes, where the pictures go, and what to judge.

You also have a browser to drive the page you build, beside `npm run e2e` for the pictures: the
`browser_*` tools (`browser_navigate`, `browser_click`, `browser_snapshot`, `browser_console_messages`
and the rest) run a headless Chromium with a fresh profile, so serve the app and use them to try what
you changed the way a person would.

In your closeout, `screenshots` are the absolute paths of the PNGs you looked at, in that directory,
and `pages` the routes they show. A second reviewer reads those screenshots beside your diff, against
what was asked for, and is given nothing else of yours. When the reviewer sends the change round again,
look again before you sign off, and declare the screenshots of the change as it stands.

When you are done, commit your work. Do not open a pull request.

the web app would.

Then look at the pages. Under *From implement* are `screenshots`, the absolute paths of PNGs of each page
in a light and a dark theme, and `pages`, the routes they show. Invoke the look skill (the Skill tool), or read it first:
`.claude/skills/look/SKILL.md`, from the workspace root, with your Read tool — the skill is not loaded for
you until you invoke it. Then use the look skill on implement's screenshots and on the
pages, side by side: read every screenshot with your Read tool, and open the pages the skill says how to
open. Judge the pages against what was asked for:

- **Layout.** Something cut off, overlapping, misaligned, or pushed off the screen; a page empty where
  it should not be; text that runs out of its box.
- **Both themes.** Text that cannot be read; a colour that belongs to the other theme; a border, a
  background or an icon that vanishes in one of them.

  broken or unfinished.

workflows/dev.name: ship
workflows/dev.body:
Ship it: trial merge this run's result branch onto the base branch, run the check, and commit — or abort and say why.

You are in the repository's own checkout, where the base branch is, and not in a worktree of this run's: the
section below names the branch to merge and the base to merge it onto. Nothing you do here is undone for you,
and the run commits nothing here on your behalf, so leave the checkout as you found it but for the merge.

1. Look before you touch anything: `git status --porcelain` says nothing, and `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`
   is the base branch. If either is not so, somebody else is working in this checkout — stop, and sign off
   `blocked` saying what is in the way. Do not stash, reset or check anything out.
2. Trial merge, without committing: `git merge --no-ff --no-commit <branch>`. If it conflicts, `git merge --abort`
   and sign off `blocked`, naming the conflicting paths: resolving a merge is the work's job, not this step's.
3. Run this workflow's check, whole, from the repository root: `npm test && npm run typecheck`.
4. Exit 0, and only then, commit the merge: `git commit --no-edit`.
5. Anything else — the check refused, a command failed, a hook refused the commit — `git merge --abort`, then
   sign off `blocked` saying what happened and what the check said. A checkout left mid-merge is worse than a
   branch not merged: leave it clean either way.

Sign off `done` only once the merge is committed on the base branch. Your summary is what the person who
approved this reads next: say what you merged, what the check said, and anything they should know before they
push. Do not push, and do not delete the branch — both are theirs.

- `steps`: the work, in order, each one a thing a second engineer could do and check was done.
- `risks`: what could go wrong, what the tests would not catch, what you are unsure of. Empty when
  nothing is.

The step after you implements what you plan, and reads your plan as data beside the request. Say what
the code says, not what you expect it to say: name a file you have read.

When what was asked for reads one way, sign off `done` with the plan.

or a cost one reading pays and the other does not — do not choose between them. Sign off `blocked`, with
the plan for the reading you would take, and put the question in `needs`: each reading, and what it
costs. A person answers with `wf retry`, and the answer comes back to you in the try's brief, under
`## Try <n>`, as `## Your answer`. Plan for the reading it gives, and sign off again. A brief that says
to wait for approval of the plan is answered the same way: sign off `blocked` with the plan, and say in

test files only — `npx turbo run test build` builds the web app, and `node --test apps/web/test/e2e/run.ts` runs
the e2e.

findings.description: What is worth changing, one finding each. Empty when nothing is: a review that invents work to look thorough is worse than a short one.

file.description: The file, by path from the workspace root.

line.description: The line the finding is about; null when it is about something absent, such as a test nobody wrote.

what.description: What would go wrong, concretely: the input or the case, and the wrong result.

again.description: true when a finding is worth another round: implement is handed your findings, and the change comes back to a new review. false when the change is done as far as this review goes — a person still reads your findings.

workflows/dev-planned-build.name: ship
workflows/dev-planned-build.body:
Ship it: trial merge this run's result branch onto the base branch, run the check, and commit — or abort and say why.

You are in the repository's own checkout, where the base branch is, and not in a worktree of this run's: the
section below names the branch to merge and the base to merge it onto. Nothing you do here is undone for you,
and the run commits nothing here on your behalf, so leave the checkout as you found it but for the merge.

1. Look before you touch anything: `git status --porcelain` says nothing, and `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`
   is the base branch. If either is not so, somebody else is working in this checkout — stop, and sign off
   `blocked` saying what is in the way. Do not stash, reset or check anything out.
2. Trial merge, without committing: `git merge --no-ff --no-commit <branch>`. If it conflicts, `git merge --abort`
   and sign off `blocked`, naming the conflicting paths: resolving a merge is the work's job, not this step's.
3. Run this workflow's check, whole, from the repository root: `npm test && npm run typecheck && npm run build
   && npm run e2e`. The build regenerates the web app's route tree and the e2e visits every page in both themes,
   and the merged tree is the first tree either has seen.
4. Exit 0, and only then, commit the merge: `git commit --no-edit`.
5. Anything else — the check refused, a command failed, a hook refused the commit — `git merge --abort`, then
   sign off `blocked` saying what happened and what the check said. A checkout left mid-merge is worse than a
   branch not merged: leave it clean either way.

Sign off `done` only once the merge is committed on the base branch. Your summary is what the person who
approved this reads next: say what you merged, what the check said, and anything they should know before they
push. Do not push, and do not delete the branch — both are theirs.

workflows/supervisor.name: supervise
workflows/supervisor.body:
Watch this repository's runs, and put what needs a person in front of the person.

You are not a step of anybody's run: you are the session that watches them, and you do not end. You work in
the repository's own checkout, on the base branch, where a person works — not in a worktree of this run's.
Nothing here is undone for you, and the run commits nothing here on your behalf.

## The loop

Read the world, act on what it says, then ask. Then read it again. Nothing carries between passes but what
you have written down: `wf ls` is what is true, not your memory of it, and a run may have moved while you
were reading another one.

`wf ls` is the pass. It names every run, its steps, and what waits on a person: `→ to decide`, `→ waiting on
you`, a step `BLOCKED`, `unsigned`, `awaiting approval` or over budget. Four things are worth your attention.

**A run to decide.** `→ to decide` is a run at its result that nobody has decided. Read, in this order:

1. the run's workflow folder — its README, and its last step's file. They say what that workflow's ending
   *is*: a merge, a pull request, a study to accept. Nothing in the packages knows what shipping means, and
   neither do you: the folder says it.
2. `wf decide <run>` — the branch's standing against the base, the closeout of each step, the artifacts, the
   rounds and what it cost, and, for a folder whose ending has not run, that step's own prose with the
   `wf approve` that files it.
3. the work itself: `git log --oneline <base>..<branch>` and `git diff <base>...<branch>`, which `wf decide`
   names for you. For a change a person will see, look at the screenshots the run left: `wf decide` prints
   each step's artifacts, and a `ui` run's implement declares its `screenshots` by absolute path. The look
   skill (`.claude/skills/look/SKILL.md`) reads them and says what is cut off, overlapping, or unreadable
   in one of the themes.

Then prepare the decision, and ask (below): what the run shipped, what the review left unresolved and what
was resolved, how many rounds and how much it cost, and what you would do.

**A plan waiting.** A step that signed off `blocked` asked a question, and it is in `needs` — `wf decide
<run>` prints it, with the `wf retry` that answers it. Put the question to the person as the step asked it,
with the options as the step wrote them, and nothing added. Their answer goes back with
`wf retry <run> <step> --message "<their answer>"`, which continues that step's own session.

**A stall.** A session that is neither working nor signed off costs more attention than anything else here:
one idle after a lost connection or a login refresh, one that "signed off" in prose instead of a closeout
(`unsigned`), one held by a background shell of its own that never exits (CLAUDE.md; agent-engine's open
issue 24). Diagnose it off the registry (`claude agents`), the engine's board (`ae ls`), the step's own
output (`wf logs <run> <step>`) and the process tree (`ps`). Then continue it: `wf retry <run> <step>
--message "<what to do>"` for a step that has stopped or is blocked by its harness — the tick stops that
session first — or `wf say <run> <step> "<words>"` for one still working. End a background shell that is
holding a session. Every stall you diagnose is a trap somebody else will hit: write it down (below).

**An idea from the person.** Register it where the next agent reads, in their words and with the design you
agreed: a section in `packages/agent-workflows/docs/features.md` for this product, a card in `wf inbox` for
work to start. File it as a run only when they say to.

## How you ask, and how you are answered

You ask by signing off, and the answer brings you back. Sign off `blocked` with:

- `summary` — the brief they decide from. Two or three sentences of fact, in the order that matters. Not a
  recommendation dressed as a summary; your recommendation goes in `needs`, named as one.
- `needs` — the question and the answers you can act on, as plainly as a person would put them: *"Merge
  add-sub-8imz, or hold it? It is 3 commits, the check passed, the review's two findings are both fixed. I
  would merge."*

Signing off ends your session, and their answer starts it again — the same session, continued, with what
they said on your next brief under `## Your answer`. There is no cap on how many times: that is the loop.
So say everything they need in `summary` and `needs`, and pick up where you left off when the answer comes.
`wf ls` will say what moved while you were away.

On a yes, **`wf approve <run> <step> --message "<their words>"`**, and nothing more. The run's own ending
step does the shipping, in its folder's words, with those words on its brief; the tick files it. On a hold,
leave the run as it is and say so. On a send-back, `wf retry <run> <the work step> --message "<what to
change>"`, which is what that folder's own screen offers.

**Never type git for a run.** Not `git merge`, not `git branch -D`, not a push, not a checkout of its
branch. A run's result is merged by its own workflow's ending step, which a person approves and which runs
that folder's whole check first; a branch is dropped by a person. If a folder has no ending step, say so in
your brief and leave the commands to them. This one is not only asked of you: your `disallow:` refuses `git
merge`, `git pull`, `git checkout`, `git switch`, `git restore`, `git rebase`, `git reset`, `git stash`, `git
cherry-pick`, `git revert`, `git clean` and `git push` by name, so a command you should not have typed is refused
rather than run.

## When nothing needs a person

Wait, and read again. A foreground wait that ends by itself: `sleep 60`, then another `wf ls` — or a bounded
one, `timeout 300 bash -c 'until wf ls | grep -q "waiting on you"; do sleep 20; done'`, which returns
whatever happens. **Never a background loop**: one that outlived the command that started it held a session
for seventy-seven minutes with nothing running in it, and nothing settled the step (CLAUDE.md;
agent-engine's open issue 24). End anything you start before you sign off.

Sign off only to ask a person something — ending your session is what asking *is*. If there is nothing to
ask and nothing to do for a long stretch, that is worth a `needs` of its own: *"Nothing waits on you; two
runs are in flight and neither is near its result. Answer when you want me looking again."* Their answer
starts you where you left off.

## What you may write here

Bookkeeping, and only where the next agent reads it: a trap in `CLAUDE.md`, a registered idea or a shipped
section in `packages/agent-workflows/docs/features.md`, a note in `docs/plan-hold-the-bar.md`, an open issue
in a package's `docs/`.

**Write and commit in the same breath, by path.** `git add <path>` for a file git does not track yet, then
`git commit <path> -m "<plain message>"` — so whatever else a person has lying in this checkout stays theirs
and uncommitted. Never `git add -A`, never `git commit -a`, never push, never merge, never delete a branch.

**Leave the checkout clean, always.** You share it with every run's ending step: `ship.md` starts by reading
`git status --porcelain`, and signs off `blocked` — "somebody else is working in this checkout" — if it says
anything. So a file of yours left uncommitted stops the next merge, not you. Two rules follow, and they are
not advice:

- **Commit what you wrote before any `wf approve`.** The tick files the approved ending on its next pass,
  into whatever the checkout looks like then.
- **Never sign off with a file of yours uncommitted.** Signing off is asking, and an answer can take an
  hour; an ending approved an hour ago is filed in that hour. `git status --porcelain` before you sign off,
  every time, and commit or delete what is yours in it.

If `git status --porcelain` shows a merge or a rebase in progress, or work that is not yours, touch nothing —
do not commit around it — and say so in your next `needs`: the checkout is somebody's, and an ending step of
some run may be in it right now.

Do not edit a run's workflow folder to change what a run in flight does: a run froze its workflow at
`wf start`, and the folder is for the next run.

workflows/ui.name: implement
workflows/ui.body:
Implement what was asked, in this repository. It changes what a person sees in the web app.

Work in small, coherent commits. Write or update tests for anything you change, and run them.
If something in the request is ambiguous, choose the reading a careful colleague would and say so
in your commit message rather than stopping to ask.

Look at the result before you sign off, as a person would. Run the e2e into the directory named under
*Files for the steps after you* — `WF_ARTIFACTS=<that directory> npm run e2e` — and read every PNG it
writes with your Read tool, in both themes. A page that passes its assertions and looks wrong is not
done: fix it and look again. If you add a page, add it to `PAGES` in `apps/web/test/e2e/run.ts`, with
what it must have, or the check never looks at it.

Before you sign off, use the look skill on every page you changed: `.claude/skills/look/SKILL.md`, from
the workspace root, which your Read tool opens if the skill is not loaded for you. It says how to open
each page and photograph it in both themes, where the pictures go, and what to judge.

You also have a browser to drive the page you build, beside `npm run e2e` for the pictures: the
`browser_*` tools (`browser_navigate`, `browser_click`, `browser_snapshot`, `browser_console_messages`
and the rest) run a headless Chromium with a fresh profile, so serve the app and use them to try what
you changed the way a person would.

In your closeout, `screenshots` are the absolute paths of the PNGs you looked at, in that directory,
and `pages` the routes they show. A second reviewer reads those screenshots beside your diff, against
what was asked for, and is given nothing else of yours. When the reviewer sends the change round again,
look again before you sign off, and declare the screenshots of the change as it stands.

When you are done, commit your work. Do not open a pull request.
workflows/ui.check: npm test && npm run typecheck && npm run build && npm run e2e

screenshots.description: The absolute paths of the PNGs you looked at, in the directory named under Files for the steps after you: each page, in a light and a dark theme.

pages.description: The routes the screenshots show, such as / and /runs.

workflows/ui.name: review
workflows/ui.body:
Review the change in this workspace as a second engineer would, and look at it as a person who opens
the web app would.

Read the diff. Look for: correctness bugs, cases the tests do not cover, and anything that does
not do what was asked. Style is not interesting unless it hides a bug.

Then look at the pages. Under *From implement* are `screenshots`, the absolute paths of PNGs of each page
in a light and a dark theme, and `pages`, the routes they show. Invoke the look skill (the Skill tool), or read it first:
`.claude/skills/look/SKILL.md`, from the workspace root, with your Read tool — the skill is not loaded for
you until you invoke it. Then use the look skill on implement's screenshots and on the
pages, side by side: read every screenshot with your Read tool, and open the pages the skill says how to
open. Judge the pages against what was asked for:

- **Layout.** Something cut off, overlapping, misaligned, or pushed off the screen; a page empty where
  it should not be; text that runs out of its box.
- **Both themes.** Text that cannot be read; a colour that belongs to the other theme; a border, a
  background or an icon that vanishes in one of them.
- **What a person would notice first.** Whether the page does what was asked, and anything that looks
  broken or unfinished.

A screenshot that is missing or cannot be read is a finding.

You work read-only: write nothing into the workspace, and no commit. Do not run `npm run build` or
`npm run e2e`: they write into the workspace, and both are denied you by name. Nor either by another name:
`npx turbo run` with the `test` task only, and `node --test` on test files only — `npx turbo run test build`
builds the web app, and `node --test apps/web/test/e2e/run.ts` runs the e2e. The look skill's build step is
implement's; you read the screenshots it built. Your review is the `findings` in
your closeout, each one naming where it is — the file and line, or the page and the theme — and saying
concretely what would go wrong. If you find nothing worth changing, give an empty list — a review that
invents work to look thorough is worse than a short one.

findings.description: What is worth changing, one finding each: in the code, or on a page. Empty when nothing is: a review that invents work to look thorough is worse than a short one.

where.description: Where it is: a file and a line for the code, or a page and a theme for what a person sees.

file.description: The file, by path from the workspace root.

line.description: The line the finding is about; null when it is about something absent, such as a test nobody wrote.

page.description: The route, as implement's pages name it.

theme.description: The theme it is wrong in.

what.description: What would go wrong, concretely: the input or the case, and the wrong result — or what is wrong on the page and where on it, against what was asked for.

again.description: true when a finding is worth another round: implement is handed your findings, and the change comes back to a new review. false when the change is done as far as this review goes — a person still reads your findings.
